blocks.raw:
<Tip>
**Pritzker Prize = architecture's Nobel.** Established 1979, one laureate annually (or team). Each laureate = one defining building you must know. From 1979 to 2026 is 47 years of choices—this is pure memorization territory. The exam tests coverage across all eras. Expect 2–3 direct Pritzker questions.
</Tip>

blocks.raw:
<Warn>
Do not assume the Pritzker prize always goes to Western architects or to formalist monuments. Japan has eight laureates (more than any country except the USA). Recent winners from China, Brazil, Chile, India, Burkina Faso, and other regions demonstrate the profession's geographic shift. The exam tests global awareness of the full laureate list, not just famous Western names.
</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<Note>
The recent shift from Western formalist monuments to Global South social practice is significant. The prize itself is changing—recognizing different values. Note milestone laureates: first woman (Hadid 2004), first African (Kéré 2022), first posthumous (Frei Otto 2015), and the geographic expansion beyond Euro-America. These "firsts" appear frequently on exams.
</Note>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Direct matching.** The LEA presents a laureate name and asks you to identify their key building, or presents a building and asks for the architect and prize year. Pure recall — no analysis required. Example pattern: "The 1995 Pritzker laureate designed a concrete church in Osaka where light enters through a cross-shaped slit. Name the architect and building."</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Era and trend identification.** The LEA asks about shifts in the prize's focus over time. Example pattern: "How do the Pritzker selections from 2010–2024 differ from those in the 1980s in terms of geography, building type, and design philosophy?" Students must identify the shift from Western formalism toward global representation and social impact.</ExamTip>

These "firsts" are high-probability exam items.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Callout>The **Pritzker Architecture Prize** is the discipline's highest honor. The LEA tests every laureate from **1979 to 2026**, expecting you to match each architect to at least one defining building. This is pure memorization territory — no conceptual shortcut replaces knowing the full list.</Callout>
